John F. Kennedy. The thirty-fifth President of the United States, he was the youngest to assume office at age forty-three. His presidency from 1961 to his assassination in 1963 was defined by Cold War crises, civil rights advocacy, and the space race, making him an enduring symbol of American aspiration.

Kennedy was born into a wealthy, prominent Irish-American family in Boston, where his father was an ambassador and patriarch of the political Kennedy clan. He served in the Navy during World War II, commanding a patrol torpedo boat called the PT-109, which was sunk by a Japanese destroyer. He was rescued after swimming for help, an experience that shaped his public image.

Elected to the House from 1947 to 1953 and then to the Senate from 1953 to 1960, both from Massachusetts, Kennedy suffered from chronic health issues including Addison's disease and chronic back pain throughout his life, unknown to the public. He defeated Richard Nixon in the 1960 presidential election in a close, televised debate that marked the emergence of television as a decisive political medium.

Delivering his famous inauguration speech in January 1961, Kennedy asked the nation, "Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country," setting a tone of idealistic public service. Yet his presidency soon encountered serious foreign policy challenges. He authorized the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in April 1961, an attempt by CIA-backed Cuban exiles to topple Fidel Castro that failed and damaged American credibility internationally.

His greatest foreign policy success came with the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962, when a thirteen-day standoff nearly brought nuclear war as the Soviet Union placed missiles in Cuba. Kennedy's blockade and backroom negotiations with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev achieved Soviet withdrawal without military conflict. At the same time, he escalated American military involvement in Vietnam, increasing the number of military advisors from about nine hundred to around sixteen thousand by the time of his death.

Kennedy faced pressure from the civil rights movement and eventually deployed federal troops to enforce desegregation at the University of Mississippi in 1962 and the University of Alabama in 1963. In June 1963, after the Birmingham campaign, he delivered a televised address embracing civil rights as a moral issue and submitted legislation that became the Civil Rights Act of 1964, passed after his death. He also signed the Nuclear Test Ban Treaty in 1963, a Cold War thaw that reduced atmospheric radiation from nuclear testing.

Kennedy supported the space race aggressively, committing the nation to landing a man on the moon by decade's end, a goal achieved in 1969. On November 22, 1963, he was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, in a motorcade whose tragic images became indelible in American memory.
